# Institutional Memory and Learning

> **Reading model:** The main path explains what the kOA ecosystem enables. The technical reference explains how kOA-Linux hosts, isolates, verifies, and operates those capabilities. Product-specific details remain in each subsystem's own documentation.

Memory is not one database. It is the reconstructable relationship between knowledge, decisions, work, evidence, culture, and later review.

The ecosystem preserves complementary forms of memory:

- **Kristal** — claims, provenance, uncertainty, semantic relations, and versions;
- **Orgo** — signals, cases, tasks, ownership, escalation, outcomes, and recurring operational patterns;
- **Konnaxion** — learning, proposals, deliberation, public outcomes, projects, and cultural participation;
- **Kreative / Konservation** — cultural works with context, rights, consent, authority, and exhibitions;
- **kOA Mediatheque** — local media and file authority;
- **governance and audit services** — policies, decisions, receipts, exceptions, and recourse;
- **kOA-Linux** — backup, restore, portability, and continuity of local operation.

Memory becomes learning when results update knowledge, procedures, curriculum, policy, and the next cycle of action.

# Knowledge-to-Action Loop

> **Reading model:** The main path explains what the kOA ecosystem enables. The technical reference explains how kOA-Linux hosts, isolates, verifies, and operates those capabilities. Product-specific details remain in each subsystem's own documentation.

## The collective cycle

```text
Know → Choose → Act → Remember → Know better
```

The expanded operational loop is:

```text
1. Observe and contribute
2. Structure meaning and preserve provenance
3. Compile reusable knowledge
4. Learn, consult, and deliberate
5. Produce explicit decision readings and outcomes
6. Convert outcomes into mandates, roles, cases, and tasks
7. Execute, escalate, close, and record evidence
8. Preserve institutional and cultural memory
9. Review results and update knowledge
```

## Systems along the loop

| Passage | Primary systems |
| --- | --- |
| Raw inputs → structured candidates | SenTient and deterministic ingestion tools |
| Structured candidates → portable knowledge | Kristal and validation workflows |
| Knowledge → learning and public collaboration | Konnaxion / KonnectED |
| Disagreement → structured deliberation | Konnaxion / Ethikos / Korum / Konsultations |
| Deliberation → multiple transparent readings | EkoH and Smart Vote |
| Accepted outcomes → organized execution | Governance rules and Orgo |
| Execution → cases, tasks, escalation, closure | Orgo |
| Results → memory and renewed knowledge | Kristal, operational records, cultural repositories, and audit evidence |
| Entire loop → local resilient operation | kOA-Linux |

## Why the transitions matter

A contribution is not automatically knowledge. Knowledge is not automatically a decision. A vote is not automatically authorization. A decision is not automatically work. Completed work is not automatically institutional learning.

Each transition requires declared authority, evidence, thresholds, roles, receipts, and a way to contest or repair the result.

## Example: a municipality

A flood-mitigation proposal can move from local reports and research, to structured knowledge, to public consultation, to a documented decision, to departmental cases and tasks, to implementation evidence, and finally to updated knowledge that improves the next planning cycle.

The value of the ecosystem is not one interface. It is the continuity of this chain.

# Operating-System Responsibilities

> **Authority and status:** This wiki is an explanatory navigation layer. The repository contracts, accepted ADRs, normative documents, and executable validators remain authoritative for kOA-Linux Operating System. Public initkoa.org pages explain the wider kOA ecosystem and the product capabilities provided by its independently documented subsystems.

## Host and deployment

- maintained Linux host and selected immutable-image mechanism;
- boot, service management and recovery environment;
- deployment profiles and overlays;
- hardware and resource envelopes;
- local storage, networks and device access.

## Security and trust

- service identities and least privilege;
- trust roots, signatures and artifact verification;
- rootless service boundaries where applicable;
- narrow privileged host operations;
- secrets, keys and data-at-rest controls;
- network and publication boundaries.

## Runtime governance

- policy bundle activation;
- authorization and disclosure checks;
- receipts for critical transitions;
- audit routing and selective evidence preservation;
- AI and external-integration restrictions.

## Lifecycle and resilience

- release sets and compatibility;
- verified activation and rollback;
- offline bundles and transport;
- backup, restore and disaster recovery;
- capability degradation and health;
- export, transfer and credible exit.

## Integration

kOA-Linux owns the boundary, not the subsystem internals. It mounts or references pinned official documentation and validates compatibility before activation.

# Modules and Submodules

> **Reading model:** The main path explains what the kOA ecosystem enables. The technical reference explains how kOA-Linux hosts, isolates, verifies, and operates those capabilities. Product-specific details remain in each subsystem's own documentation.

## Navigation principle

This Wiki names the major systems so readers can understand the full operating cycle. It does not duplicate their internal documentation. Follow the linked product Wikis and repositories for detailed models, routes, schemas, services, and user workflows.

## Konnaxion

[Konnaxion Wiki](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/Konnaxion/wiki)

## Orgo

[Orgo Wiki](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/Orgo/wiki)

Orgo owns the operational chain from signals to Cases and Tasks, functional routing, reactivity windows, escalation, closure, insights, and cyclical review.

## Semantic and language systems

| System | Detailed documentation | Role in the ecosystem |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Kristal** | [Repository](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/kristal-framework), [public overview](https://initkoa.org/technology/kristal) | portable, verifiable, status-aware knowledge artifacts and offline runtime packs |
| **SenTient** | [Repository](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/SenTient), [public overview](https://initkoa.org/technology/sentient) | optional reconciliation, entity linking, extraction, and ambiguity-preserving candidate production |
| **SemantiK Architect** | [Wiki](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/SemantiK_Architect/wiki), [public overview](https://initkoa.org/technology/architect) | deterministic multilingual realization from structured meaning |

## Runtime, governance, and storage

- **kOA-Linux Operating System** — sovereign local runtime, profiles, isolation, trust, resources, lifecycle, offline continuity, backup, and recovery.
- **Governance Policy Runtime** — policy evaluation for authorization, disclosure, consent, exceptions, and governed transitions.
- **kOA Mediatheque** — local, private-by-default authority for files and media held by the installation.
- **UCKK** — external Moodle platform for online learning and dissemination; exchange is explicit and does not make UCKK a local subsystem.

## External and symbolic layers

Additional tools, narrative systems, and partner platforms may connect to the ecosystem, but they do not silently become authority. The symbolic layer helps make the architecture memorable and transmissible; it does not determine rights, decisions, or host privilege.

# Multilingual Knowledge Networks

> **Authority and status:** This wiki is an explanatory navigation layer. The repository contracts, accepted ADRs, normative documents, and executable validators remain authoritative for kOA-Linux Operating System. Public initkoa.org pages explain the wider kOA ecosystem and the product capabilities provided by its independently documented subsystems.

## Intended environment

Several communities or institutions can share structured knowledge while using different languages, terminology and authority channels. The underlying meaning and provenance remain portable; each reader receives a policy-selected rendering appropriate to the available language resources.

## Capability chain

1. Kristal carries structured assertions, provenance, scope and authority.
2. Reader policy selects the permitted view.
3. Semantik Architect renders the selected meaning in a target language.
4. Ariane exposes actions and navigation labels semantically.
5. Konnaxion distributes the resulting knowledge surface.
6. kOA-Linux activates the required packs locally and supports offline use.

## Non-equivalence and disagreement

A term without an exact translation should remain explicitly mapped or unresolved. The system must preserve disputed meanings and authority-scoped language rather than forcing every community into one vocabulary.

- [Semantik Architect](https://initkoa.org/technology/architect)
- [Kristal](https://initkoa.org/technology/kristal)

# Multilingual Operation

> **Authority and status:** This wiki is an explanatory navigation layer. The repository contracts, accepted ADRs, normative documents, and executable validators remain authoritative for kOA-Linux Operating System. Public initkoa.org pages explain the wider kOA ecosystem and the product capabilities provided by its independently documented subsystems.

## More than interface translation

The multilingual objective is to preserve meaning across languages, not merely replace strings. A governance decision, role description, uncertainty label or knowledge assertion must not become stronger, weaker or less qualified because it is rendered in another language.

## Semantik Architect

Semantik Architect separates structured meaning from language-specific realization. It uses semantic frames, constructions, language-family engines, language profiles, lexicons, render profiles and regression tests to produce deterministic text.

It may render:

- role and mandate summaries;
- decision explanations;
- knowledge query results;
- civic process descriptions;
- multilingual cards, snippets, reports and notices;
- localized labels for Ariane-assisted navigation.

It must not invent facts absent from the selected structured input.

## Operational chain

```text
structured, policy-selected meaning
+ active language artifact
+ render profile
+ reader policy
= rendered text
+ trace metadata
```

## Language artifacts in kOA-Linux

The operating system verifies and activates compiled language artifacts. A user profile can load only the languages required for its context, while build systems produce and test heavier artifacts separately.

## Important limits

Multilingual capability depends on available lexicons, constructions, grammar resources and quality tests. A missing language resource must be exposed as a limitation; the system must not silently substitute unreviewed machine translation for a governed deterministic rendering.

## Sources

- [Semantik Architect](https://initkoa.org/technology/architect)
- [docs/02-system/13-language-system-boundary.md](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/kOA-Linux/blob/main/docs/02-system/13-language-system-boundary.md)
- [docs/06-lifecycle/09-language-artifacts.md](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/kOA-Linux/blob/main/docs/06-lifecycle/09-language-artifacts.md)

# Municipality and Public Service

> **Authority and status:** This wiki is an explanatory navigation layer. The repository contracts, accepted ADRs, normative documents, and executable validators remain authoritative for kOA-Linux Operating System. Public initkoa.org pages explain the wider kOA ecosystem and the product capabilities provided by its independently documented subsystems.

## Intended environment

A municipality or public-service organization can separate public participation from private operational handling. Konnaxion receives knowledge, proposals and civic input; governance rules define legitimate decisions; Orgo routes service requests and decisions to accountable departments.

## Example flow

```text
citizen report
→ public or private intake
→ case classification
→ responsible municipal function
→ response window
→ escalation if overdue
→ recorded outcome
→ public update when disclosure policy permits
```

## Benefits of the architecture

- public transparency without exposing private case details;
- continuity when staff change;
- offline operation for field offices;
- multilingual public explanations;
- traceable decisions and appeal paths;
- portable institutional memory.

- [Orgo guarantees](https://initkoa.org/platforms/orgo/guarantees)
- [Konnaxion](https://initkoa.org/platforms/konnaxion)

# Naming and Scope

> **Reading model:** The main path explains what the kOA ecosystem enables. The technical reference explains how kOA-Linux hosts, isolates, verifies, and operates those capabilities. Product-specific details remain in each subsystem's own documentation.

## Four scopes

### kOA initiative

The broader body of theory, civic principles, cultural work, research, narrative, and institutional proposals.

### kOA ecosystem

The interoperating digital systems that support the cycle from knowledge to deliberation, decision, execution, and memory.

### kOA-Linux Operating System

The sovereign runtime and deployment environment. It hosts selected capabilities and enforces local isolation, resources, trust, lifecycle, offline behavior, recovery, and integration boundaries.

### Product systems and modules

Konnaxion, Orgo, Kristal, Ariane, SenTient, SemantiK Architect, and other products retain their own internal documentation and authority. Konnaxion also contains named modules and submodules documented in its own Wiki.

## Naming rule

This Wiki must not use **kOA-Linux** as a synonym for the complete kOA ecosystem. It may explain the ecosystem because the operating system exists to run it, but it must always identify which product owns a capability.

UCKK is an external Moodle platform, not an internal kOA-Linux subsystem. The local kOA Mediatheque and UCKK exchange remain secondary infrastructure topics, not the definition of the ecosystem.

# Offline-First Operation

> **Reading model:** The main path explains what the kOA ecosystem enables. The technical reference explains how kOA-Linux hosts, isolates, verifies, and operates those capabilities. Product-specific details remain in each subsystem's own documentation.

Offline capability is a governance guarantee: a community should be able to preserve local knowledge, work, evidence, and continuity without permanent dependence on a cloud provider.

Depending on the active profile, local operation can include:

- Kristal knowledge and provenance;
- Ariane navigation graphs;
- Konnaxion portable resources and selected local spaces;
- Orgo cases, tasks, routing, and queues;
- kOA Mediatheque files and imported learning packages;
- deterministic multilingual rendering with installed artifacts;
- local policy evaluation, backup, and recovery.

External publication, remote discovery, federation, and optional AI services wait for connectivity. The system must show what is local, queued, stale, unavailable, or awaiting review.

# Operations

> **Authority notice:** This wiki is a readable navigation layer. Source contracts, accepted ADRs, normative documents, and executable validators in the repository remain authoritative.

## Operating model

Operations preserve declared authority, evidence, recoverability, resource bounds, and profile-specific guarantees. A node remains locally authoritative for final admission and sensitive host mutations.

## Operational domains

| Domain | Main concerns |
| --- | --- |
| Observability | Health, readiness, events, receipts, metrics, and bounded diagnostics |
| Resources | CPU, memory, I/O, concurrency, queues, scheduling, and capacity |
| Continuity | Offline operation, safe degradation, backup, restore, and disaster recovery |
| Incidents | Detection, containment, evidence, repair, communication, and recourse |
| Maintenance | Verified updates, storage care, key rotation, cleanup, and lifecycle tasks |
| Profile operations | User-lightweight, sovereign-node, hub, control-plane, and build-farm procedures |

## Backup and restore

Backups preserve authoritative data, contracts, keys or key references, manifests, provenance, and verification evidence according to the active profile. Restore is tested and does not silently merge incompatible authority states.

# Portable Knowledge with Kristal

> **Authority and status:** This wiki is an explanatory navigation layer. The repository contracts, accepted ADRs, normative documents, and executable validators remain authoritative for kOA-Linux Operating System. Public initkoa.org pages explain the wider kOA ecosystem and the product capabilities provided by its independently documented subsystems.

## What a Kristal provides

A Kristal is a portable, verifiable epistemic artifact. It allows knowledge to move between people, organizations and systems while keeping provenance, integrity, assertion status, certainty, authority, scope and reader policy visible.

The purpose is not to label every statement as universally true. A Kristal can preserve uncertainty, disagreement, symbolic material, research claims and scoped recognition without flattening them into one confidence score.

## User outcomes

A person or organization can:

- carry a knowledge package between systems;
- verify the package locally;
- browse and query it without a central server;
- inspect sources and status;
- compare versions;
- combine knowledge from several authorities without silently merging their claims;
- preserve durable references that do not depend on a live webpage.

## Offline Runtime Packs

A Runtime Pack is a read-optimized package for local browsing and query. The canonical exchange and provenance remain distinct from the local runtime projection. When verification fails or a pack is outdated, the system exposes that status rather than silently treating it as current authority.

## Role of kOA-Linux Operating System

The operating system stores, verifies, activates, pins, updates and rolls back Runtime Packs. It also enforces resource limits and reader/disclosure policy at the local boundary.

- [Kristal](https://initkoa.org/technology/kristal)

# Release and Artifact Lifecycle

> **Authority notice:** This wiki is a readable navigation layer. Source contracts, accepted ADRs, normative documents, and executable validators in the repository remain authoritative.

## Lifecycle model

Artifacts are identified, verified, staged, activated, observed, recovered, retained, and removed through declared contracts. Activation is atomic or otherwise fail-safe for the applicable artifact class.

An activation failure leaves the current verified release active. Recovery restores the latest verified release as one unit; it does not activate an undeclared operating mode.

## Core lifecycle stages

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    BUILD[Build] --> VERIFY[Verify]
    VERIFY --> STAGE[Stage]
    STAGE --> AUTHORIZE[Authorize]
    AUTHORIZE --> ACTIVATE[Activate]
    ACTIVATE --> OBSERVE[Observe]
    OBSERVE -->|failure| RECOVER[Recover or forward repair]
    OBSERVE --> RETAIN[Retain or remove by policy]
```

## Artifact contracts

| Artifact or exchanged object | Schema |
| --- | --- |
| kOA Cultural Rights Policy Artifact | [schema](../blob/main/docs/contracts/artifact-contracts/cultural-rights-policy.schema.json) |

## Release controls

- release channels are independently versioned;
- a release set pins compatible identities;
- signatures, provenance, SBOM, compatibility, policy, and evidence are checked before activation;
- offline bundles preserve verification and admission rules;
- data schema evolution and contract removal remain explicit;
- forward repair is preferred when rollback would violate data or compatibility constraints.

# Roles, Tasks, and Accountability

> **Authority and status:** This wiki is an explanatory navigation layer. The repository contracts, accepted ADRs, normative documents, and executable validators remain authoritative for kOA-Linux Operating System. Public initkoa.org pages explain the wider kOA ecosystem and the product capabilities provided by its independently documented subsystems.

## Function-first coordination

Orgo routes work to responsibilities such as Intake, Incident Response, Procurement, Legal Review, Case Management or Maintenance. This reduces dependence on whoever happens to read a message and preserves continuity when people leave or teams reorganize.

## Roles

A role represents a durable responsibility with scoped permissions. People may be assigned to roles for an organization, team, location, unit or other declared scope. Role assignments are revocable and auditable.

## Cases

A case is the durable context for a situation: why work exists, which policy applies, who owns it, which artifacts are linked, what tasks belong to it, and how the outcome can be reviewed.

## Tasks

A task is an executable unit of work with:

- identity and parent case;
- owning role or person;
- status and allowed transitions;
- inputs and expected outputs;
- deadline and retry limits;
- approval and capability gates;
- visibility and confidentiality;
- evidence and completion criteria.

## Escalation and closure

An overdue task does not disappear silently. Policy determines when responsibility escalates and who is notified. Closure records the result, actors, changes, evidence and unresolved matters.

## Organizational learning

Recurring delays, duplicates, failures or policy friction can become new review or audit cases. The system therefore converts operational patterns into governed improvement work.

## Sources

- [What Orgo does](https://initkoa.org/platforms/orgo/what-it-does)
- [Routing and escalation](https://initkoa.org/platforms/orgo/routing-escalation)
- [Core guarantees](https://initkoa.org/platforms/orgo/guarantees)
- [docs/contracts/subsystems/orgo.subsystem.json](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/kOA-Linux/blob/main/docs/contracts/subsystems/orgo.subsystem.json)

# Security Model

> **Authority notice:** This wiki is a readable navigation layer. Source contracts, accepted ADRs, normative documents, and executable validators in the repository remain authoritative.

## Security posture

kOA uses explicit trust, least privilege, compartmentalized authority, signed artifacts, narrow privileged interfaces, bounded integrations, and recoverable failure states.

## Major security boundaries

- identity and trust roots;
- profile-scoped privilege and service identities;
- network and storage isolation;
- encrypted data and key handling;
- AI and external-integration boundaries;
- privacy, disclosure, consent, and cultural rights;
- selective audit and evidence access;
- cross-domain publication;
- offline import and software supply chain;
- break-glass authority with receipts and review.

## Privileged operations

The kOA Node Agent exposes closed high-level operations rather than arbitrary shell, package, file, container, service-manager, device, or private-key interfaces. The active node performs final local validation before a sensitive mutation.

## Disclosure and audit

Audit is selective. Evidence access follows policy, purpose, identity, disclosure class, and recourse rules. Auditability does not imply unrestricted transparency.

# Semantic Sovereignty

> **Authority and status:** This wiki is an explanatory navigation layer. The repository contracts, accepted ADRs, normative documents, and executable validators remain authoritative for kOA-Linux Operating System. Public initkoa.org pages explain the wider kOA ecosystem and the product capabilities provided by its independently documented subsystems.

## The problem

Systems often centralize meaning in one vendor's database, ranking model, taxonomy, language model, or interface vocabulary. When definitions, confidence, authority and disagreement are hidden, users can no longer tell what a statement means, where it came from, or which institution recognizes it.

Semantic sovereignty means that meaning remains **portable, inspectable, governed and revisable**.

## What must remain explicit

- terminology and concept identifiers;
- provenance and evidence references;
- assertion status and certainty;
- authority channel and recognition scope;
- disputed, symbolic, fictional, mythological or research status;
- reader policy and disclosure constraints;
- multilingual mappings and non-equivalent terms;
- version history and supersession.

## Systems involved

### Kristal

Kristal packages structured epistemic state so knowledge can be verified, queried, distributed and preserved without pretending that every assertion has universal authority.

### Semantik Architect

Architect renders the selected structured meaning into language. It must not make a statement appear more certain, factual, validated or universal than the input allows.

### Ariane

Ariane represents the meaning and action structure of interfaces, allowing navigation by function rather than by fragile visual coordinates alone.

### SenTient

SenTient may help reconcile ambiguous or messy inputs, but its output remains candidate material until separately reviewed and validated.

## Role of the operating system

kOA-Linux verifies and activates the relevant artifacts, keeps versions visible, applies reader and disclosure policy, and ensures that optional AI cannot silently replace governed semantics.

## Sources

- [Kristal](https://initkoa.org/technology/kristal)
- [Semantik Architect](https://initkoa.org/technology/architect)
- [Ariane](https://initkoa.org/technology/ariane)
- [docs/01-constitution/03-system-principles.md](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/kOA-Linux/blob/main/docs/01-constitution/03-system-principles.md)
- [docs/02-system/13-language-system-boundary.md](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/kOA-Linux/blob/main/docs/02-system/13-language-system-boundary.md)

# SemantiK Architect

> **Reading model:** The main path explains what the kOA ecosystem enables. The technical reference explains how kOA-Linux hosts, isolates, verifies, and operates those capabilities. Product-specific details remain in each subsystem's own documentation.

SemantiK Architect is the multilingual meaning-realization system. It produces deterministic language output from structured meaning while preserving status, scope, provenance, and disagreement.

Use:

- [SemantiK Architect GitHub Wiki](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/SemantiK_Architect/wiki)
- [Repository](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/SemantiK_Architect)
- [Public overview](https://initkoa.org/technology/architect)

kOA-Linux activates verified language artifacts and supplies runtime isolation and resources. It does not duplicate grammar, lexicon, construction, or QA specifications.

# Siloed and Sovereign Environments

> **Authority and status:** This wiki is an explanatory navigation layer. The repository contracts, accepted ADRs, normative documents, and executable validators remain authoritative for kOA-Linux Operating System. Public initkoa.org pages explain the wider kOA ecosystem and the product capabilities provided by its independently documented subsystems.

## What “silo” means here

A silo is not automatically a defect. A community, organization, institution, field team, municipality, or high-assurance unit may need its own data, identities, rules, storage, availability and authority. The problem is not separation itself; the problem is separation without safe interoperability, portability or exit.

kOA-Linux Operating System is designed to support **bounded environments that can cooperate without becoming one shared database or one central authority**.

## Isolation dimensions

A deployment can separate:

- identities and role assignments;
- databases and authoritative stores;
- files, media and encryption keys;
- service accounts and host privileges;
- network segments and outbound access;
- policy bundles and trust roots;
- release channels and activation schedules;
- audit visibility and evidence access;
- synchronization and publication gateways.

## Interoperability between silos

Cooperation happens through declared objects and transitions:

- Kristals and other portable artifacts;
- signed or verified bundles;
- publication gateways;
- Orgo signals, cases, tasks and receipts;
- explicit synchronization sessions;
- scoped identity and trust assertions;
- controlled exports and imports.

Direct writes into another subsystem's authoritative database are prohibited by the architecture.

## Deployment patterns

### Independent organization

One organization runs a local node with private Orgo services, local files, selected knowledge packs and controlled external publication.

### Community hub

A hub serves local users, distributes knowledge and civic surfaces, and synchronizes when connectivity is available.

### Federated institutions

Several institutions maintain separate authorities but exchange verified artifacts and accountable requests.

### Air-gapped environment

Updates and exports travel through removable media or controlled transfer, with local verification before activation.

## Safe failure behavior

A missing remote system does not justify broadening access or substituting a different provider. The system preserves queued work, visible version state and explicit unavailable/degraded labels.

## Sources

- [docs/01-constitution/07-component-separation.md](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/kOA-Linux/blob/main/docs/01-constitution/07-component-separation.md)
- [docs/02-system/04-component-boundaries.md](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/kOA-Linux/blob/main/docs/02-system/04-component-boundaries.md)
- [docs/07-security/02-security-domains.md](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/kOA-Linux/blob/main/docs/07-security/02-security-domains.md)
- [docs/07-security/08-network-boundaries.md](https://github.com/Rejean-McCormick/kOA-Linux/blob/main/docs/07-security/08-network-boundaries.md)
- [Kristal portability and offline use](https://initkoa.org/technology/kristal/portability-and-offline)

# Societal Outcomes

> **Reading model:** The main path explains what the kOA ecosystem enables. The technical reference explains how kOA-Linux hosts, isolates, verifies, and operates those capabilities. Product-specific details remain in each subsystem's own documentation.

## Collective capacity

The principal outcome is not engagement. It is the ability of a group to organize knowledge, clarify disagreement, make legitimate choices, coordinate execution, and preserve reconstructable memory.

## Democratic infrastructure

kOA treats discoverability, credibility, classification, deliberation, decision protocols, accountability, and memory as political infrastructure. These functions shape what a public can see, compare, decide, and act upon.

To avoid technocracy, equal political standing and advisory competence signals remain distinct. EkoH and Smart Vote can provide domain-bounded readings without silently replacing the baseline decision result.

## Non-domination

A system is not legitimate merely because it coordinates efficiently. People and communities must be able to understand, contest, repair, export, self-host, fork, or leave the infrastructure they depend on.

This is why offline capability, fail-closed integrity, auditability, portability, explicit authority, and semantic sovereignty are social and political requirements—not only technical features.

## Social cohesion without uniformity

Social cohesion does not require everyone to agree. It requires enough shared, inspectable reference points to distinguish evidence, uncertainty, value conflicts, decisions, responsibilities, and results.

The system aims to make plurality governable rather than erase it.

## Cultural sovereignty

Culture cannot be protected by storage alone. Cultural memory requires provenance, context, creator and community authority, consent, rights, restrictions, review, withdrawal, and governance pathways.

Kreative and Konservation provide the relevant cultural layer inside Konnaxion. See [Cultural Sovereignty](Cultural-Sovereignty).

## Institutional continuity

Cases, tasks, decisions, receipts, versions, provenance, and post-action review allow organizations and communities to retain knowledge when people, mandates, or platforms change.

## Global-local collaboration

The architecture supports globally reusable knowledge and locally governed action. A community can share selected artifacts while keeping local deliberation, private work, cultural restrictions, or organizational operations within its own authority.

# Sociotechnical Operating System

> **Reading model:** The main path explains what the kOA ecosystem enables. The technical reference explains how kOA-Linux hosts, isolates, verifies, and operates those capabilities. Product-specific details remain in each subsystem's own documentation.

## Governance as runtime

A conventional platform hosts content or interaction. A **Sociotechnical Operating System** runs the combined social and technical rules that make collective action possible:

- roles and permissions;
- integrity and validation rules;
- decision protocols;
- accountability workflows;
- audit and recourse;
- semantic and language infrastructure;
- operational routing, escalation, and closure;
- local and offline continuity.

The social structure is not an external policy document added after the software is built. Roles, norms, authority, consent, and review are part of the operating model.

## Why a system of systems

No single platform should own knowledge, public deliberation, organizational execution, language, culture, identity, media, and host privilege at once. kOA separates these functions into systems with explicit boundaries.

This supports **integration without contamination**: systems exchange artifacts, requests, events, and receipts without silently absorbing each other's authority or databases.

## Conditions of legitimacy

Operational power is acceptable only when it remains:

- inspectable and auditable;
- contestable and revisable;
- explicit about the difference between credibility and decision result;
- portable and locally operable;
- resistant to platform capture;
- multilingual without flattening differences;
- bounded by consent, rights, and cultural authority;
- capable of safe failure rather than hidden substitution.

## Role of kOA-Linux

kOA-Linux is the technical runtime beneath this social architecture. It supplies the host-level conditions—profiles, isolation, trust, resources, activation, offline behavior, backup, and recovery—without claiming ownership of the product logic of Konnaxion, Orgo, Ariane, SemantiK Architect, SenTient, or other independent systems.

# System Architecture

> **Authority notice:** This wiki is a readable navigation layer. Source contracts, accepted ADRs, normative documents, and executable validators in the repository remain authoritative.

## System class

The system contract defines kOA as a local-first, offline-capable, modular operating environment for governed knowledge, coordination, language, media, navigation, publication, and sovereign deployment.

## Architectural layers

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    C["L0 — Constitutional principles"]
    S["L1 — System baseline"]
    P["L2 — Deployment profiles"]
    X["L3 — Internal component and subsystem-boundary contracts"]
    R["L4 — Non-normative implementation recipes"]
    C --> S --> P --> X --> R
```

## Operating modes

| Mode | Purpose | Connectivity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `interactive_user` | Operate the local user-facing kOA environment with deterministic core services and task-activated heavy work. | online, restricted_network, offline |
| `development` | Develop multiple kOA applications, branches, and worktrees in isolated reproducible workspaces. | online, restricted_network |
| `build` | Produce reproducible, validated, provenance-bearing system, service, governance, and knowledge artifacts. | online, restricted_network, offline_with_imported_sources |
| `service_node` | Host a persistent kOA node with profile-defined availability, security, recovery, and offline guarantees. | online, restricted_network, offline |
| `hub` | Coordinate multiple nodes, artifacts, or governed domains without replacing component or node authority. | online, restricted_network, intermittent |
| `control_plane` | Operate deployment, release, policy, and fleet coordination services for profiles that require a control plane. | online, restricted_network |
| `recovery` | Restore a valid system, artifact set, or authoritative data state without creating partial authority. | online, restricted_network, offline |

## Boundary rules

- Components do not write directly into another component or subsystem's authoritative state.
- Privileged host mutations pass through narrow, declared interfaces.
- External integrations are optional, capability-scoped, and non-authoritative.
- Profile contracts select deployment membership, resources, connectivity, and degradation behavior.
- Release and artifact identity must agree before activation.

# A System of Systems

> **Reading model:** The main path explains what the kOA ecosystem enables. The technical reference explains how kOA-Linux hosts, isolates, verifies, and operates those capabilities. Product-specific details remain in each subsystem's own documentation.

## Why not one platform

The architecture spans public collaboration, organizational execution, validated knowledge, semantics, language, interfaces, culture, governance, storage, identity, and infrastructure. One monolith would concentrate excessive authority and become difficult to evolve or exit.

kOA therefore separates product ownership while connecting the products through a common knowledge-to-action cycle.

## Ecosystem map

| Layer | Systems and modules | Primary role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Knowledge and semantic artifacts | Kristal, SenTient | structured knowledge, provenance, candidate reconciliation, portability |
| Public learning and collaboration | Konnaxion / KonnectED, keenKonnect, Kreative | learning, projects, culture, public participation, creation |
| Deliberation and judgment | Ethikos, Korum, Konsultations, EkoH, Smart Vote | disagreement mapping, consultation, decision procedures, advisory readings |
| Organizational execution | Orgo | signals, cases, tasks, roles, routing, escalation, closure, insights |
| Language and navigation | SemantiK Architect, Ariane | multilingual realization, semantic interfaces, assisted navigation |
| Local media and exchange | kOA Mediatheque, optional external UCKK exchange | local private media authority and explicit learning-content exchange |
| Governance and trust | Governance runtime, identity, audit, receipts | authorization, disclosure, consent, recourse, evidence |
| Sovereign runtime | kOA-Linux | profiles, isolation, resources, activation, offline continuity, recovery |

## Cooperation rules

1. Each system owns its internal state and product rules.
2. Exchanges use explicit artifacts, APIs, events, tasks, and receipts.
3. Advisory credibility signals do not silently become sovereign decisions.
4. Optional AI does not create invisible authority.
5. Failure of one system does not authorize another to absorb its role.
6. Local autonomy and global interoperability coexist through portable, governed exchanges.

See [Modules and Submodules](Modules-and-Submodules) and [Related Wikis](Related-Wikis).

# kOA and UCKK Mediatheques

> **Reading model:** The main path explains what the kOA ecosystem enables. The technical reference explains how kOA-Linux hosts, isolates, verifies, and operates those capabilities. Product-specific details remain in each subsystem's own documentation.

The Mediatheque relationship is one infrastructure topic inside the larger ecosystem.

- **kOA Mediatheque** — local, private-by-default, offline authority for media and files held by the installation.
- **UCKK Mediatheque** — online authority for content accepted by the external UCKK Moodle platform.

They may implement compatible frames for identity, versions, hashes, metadata, provenance, rights, restrictions, relations, collections, languages, renditions, and lifecycle. Compatibility does not create a shared database, shared authority, or automatic synchronization.

See [Files, Media, and Provenance](Files-Media-and-Provenance) and [UCKK](UCKK).

# UCKK

> **Reading model:** The main path explains what the kOA ecosystem enables. The technical reference explains how kOA-Linux hosts, isolates, verifies, and operates those capabilities. Product-specific details remain in each subsystem's own documentation.

UCKK is an external Moodle platform for online learning, courses, pathways, activities, resources, and learning communities.

It is not an internal kOA-Linux subsystem and does not define the kOA ecosystem. Its own Mediatheque is distinct from the local kOA Mediatheque.

Where enabled, kOA-Linux can support two explicit operations:

- `publish_to_uckk` — publish an authorized local representation as a distinct UCKK object;
- `import_from_uckk` — import a selected UCKK resource as a distinct local offline copy.

There is no implicit database merge or generic `sync_mediatheques` operation.

# Use Cases

> **Reading model:** The main path explains what the kOA ecosystem enables. The technical reference explains how kOA-Linux hosts, isolates, verifies, and operates those capabilities. Product-specific details remain in each subsystem's own documentation.

## Education

Schools can use portable knowledge, multilingual resources, local media, and offline packages. Learners can move from study to collaborative projects, while credentials, provenance, and local adaptations remain governed.

## Municipal and civic action

Residents, experts, and officials can build shared knowledge around an issue, deliberate proposals, preserve multiple readings, make an explicit decision, route implementation through accountable roles, and publish evidence of progress.

## Organizational operations

An organization can turn email, forms, reports, incidents, and decisions into Cases and Tasks with owners, reactivity windows, escalation, closure, and recurring review through Orgo.

## Research and innovation

Researchers can combine sources, datasets, candidate extraction, semantic artifacts, project workspaces, blueprints, validation, and reusable outputs. Knowledge produced in one project can become a portable input for another.

## Cultural memory and collaboration

Artists, communities, archives, and institutions can document works with provenance, rights, consent, context, exhibitions, trust signals, collaboration spaces, and governance workflows through Kreative and Konservation.

## Crisis and field operations

A local node can retain procedures, knowledge, files, tasks, identity, and recovery capabilities during network failure. Remote exchange waits; local authority and evidence remain available.

## Global-local networks

Global collaboration can produce shared artifacts and reference models, while local nodes decide what to adopt, adapt, publish, keep private, or reject.

# What kOA Does

> **Reading model:** The main path explains what the kOA ecosystem enables. The technical reference explains how kOA-Linux hosts, isolates, verifies, and operates those capabilities. Product-specific details remain in each subsystem's own documentation.

## The direct answer

kOA helps a collective govern the full cycle through which it knows, chooses, acts, and remembers.

It does not assume that more information automatically creates better decisions, or that participation automatically creates action. Each transition is treated as a governed transformation:

- contributions require interpretation and provenance before becoming knowledge;
- knowledge requires deliberation and explicit procedures before informing a decision;
- decisions require mandates, owners, resources, and tasks before becoming action;
- action requires evidence and review before becoming durable memory;
- memory must remain reusable so the next cycle starts from accumulated learning rather than institutional amnesia.

## Five operating questions

The ecosystem is organized around five questions:

1. What is reliable enough to act on?
2. How can disagreement become legible instead of collapsing into noise?
3. How can judgment improve without expertise becoming sovereign power?
4. How do decisions become responsibilities, tasks, escalation, closure, and learning?
5. How can the entire chain be reconstructed, contested, repaired, and reused later?

## What this produces

When the chain works, a group can:

- build and share verified knowledge;
- learn across languages and locations;
- deliberate without losing evidence or minority positions;
- distinguish equal democratic standing from advisory competence signals;
- convert outcomes into accountable organizational work;
- preserve cultural and institutional memory;
- operate locally during network failure;
- remain able to inspect, contest, export, fork, or leave the infrastructure it depends on.

kOA is therefore not primarily a content platform. It is infrastructure for **controlled transformation from knowledge to collective capacity**.

# What kOA-Linux Operating System Does

> **Reading model:** The main path explains what the kOA ecosystem enables. The technical reference explains how kOA-Linux hosts, isolates, verifies, and operates those capabilities. Product-specific details remain in each subsystem's own documentation.

## Its role in the big picture

kOA-Linux does not implement the entire sociotechnical ecosystem. It provides the sovereign runtime in which selected systems can operate together without collapsing their authority boundaries.

## Responsibilities

- run profile-selected capabilities locally;
- isolate identities, services, stores, networks, keys, and privilege;
- verify and activate software, policy, language, and knowledge artifacts;
- allocate CPU, memory, storage, queues, and background work;
- preserve declared offline behavior and safe degradation;
- provide backup, restore, recovery, export, and credible exit;
- control publication, import, AI, and external-integration boundaries;
- preserve audit evidence and receipts for critical transitions.

## What it does not own

kOA-Linux does not define Konnaxion's civic modules, Orgo's internal workflows, SemantiK grammar construction, SenTient's reconciliation pipeline, Ariane's full navigation model, or UCKK's Moodle internals. Those belong to their owning products and Wikis.

Use [Related Wikis](Related-Wikis) for product detail and [Technical Reference](Technical-Reference) for the operating-system architecture.
